GRANDPARENT VISITATION (PETITION INFORMATION SHEET)
Prepared for Casey Lee · Riley Lee

PETITIONING GRANDPARENT — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION
I, Casey Lee, am the grandparent of Riley Lee, a minor born May 3, 2015. My relationship to Riley Lee is: Paternal grandmother. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual grandparent-visitation petition, to be filed in California superior court under Family Code § 3102, § 3103, or § 3104, whichever applies to this family's circumstances. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant Casey Lee — or any grandparent — visitation rights with Riley Lee. Riley Lee's parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Lee, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the applicable statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can actually grant grandparent visitation.

THIS PETITION INFORMATION SHEET DESCRIBES A COURT PROCEEDING, NOT A GRANT OF VISITATION
California law lets a grandparent seek court-ordered visitation with Riley Lee only through one of several distinct statutory pathways in the Family Code's chapter on visitation rights (Fam. Code §§ 3100-3105) — not through a private agreement, letter, or this information sheet itself. The general, freestanding pathway, Family Code § 3104(a), provides: "On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court" makes certain findings described in this document's companion clauses. Completing this information sheet does not itself grant Casey Lee — or any grandparent — visitation rights with Riley Lee; only a court order issued after a petition, notice, and hearing under the applicable statute can do that.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court does both of the following: (1) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the grandparent and the grandchild that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child. (2) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the grandparent against the right of the parents to exercise their parental authority."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that grandparent visitation in California arises only from an actual court petition and order, never from a private document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. California actually provides three distinct statutory pathways for grandparent visitation depending on the family's circumstances (a deceased parent under § 3102, a pending custody proceeding between the parents under § 3103, or a freestanding petition under § 3104), each with its own requirements; this clause describes only the shared framework, and this document's companion clauses address each pathway's specific requirements separately. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 3104(a)); no additional independent source was found for this framing.

GRANDPARENT VISITATION WHEN A PARENT HAS DIED — FAMILY CODE § 3102
If a parent of Riley Lee, an unemancipated minor, is deceased, California Family Code § 3102(a) allows not only the deceased parent's own parents (that is, Riley Lee's grandparents) but also the deceased parent's children, siblings, and other parent to petition for reasonable visitation with Riley Lee during Riley Lee's minority, upon a finding that the visitation would be in Riley Lee's best interest. Where the court grants visitation under this section to someone other than a grandparent of the child, § 3102(b) directs the court to consider the amount of personal contact that person had with the child before the visitation application was filed. Under § 3102(c), this section does not apply — and any visitation rights already granted under it automatically terminate — if the child has been adopted by someone other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If either parent of an unemancipated minor child is deceased, the children, siblings, parents, and grandparents of the deceased parent may be granted reasonable visitation with the child during the child's minority upon a finding that the visitation would be in the best interest of the minor child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3102(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3102.)
  "In granting visitation pursuant to this section to a person other than a grandparent of the child, the court shall consider the amount of personal contact between the person and the child before the application for the visitation order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3102(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3102.)
  "This section does not apply if the child has been adopted by a person other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child. Any visitation rights granted pursuant to this section before the adoption of the child automatically terminate if the child is adopted by a person other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3102(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3102.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's deceased-parent grandparent (and other-relative) visitation mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3102(a), (b), and (c)); no additional independent source beyond § 3102 itself was found for this. This corrects an assumption embedded in the research request that prompted this clause: § 3102's petitioning class is broader than grandparents alone — its actual text also reaches the deceased parent's own children, siblings, and surviving parent (so, for example, a minor child's aunts, uncles, or adult siblings could also qualify to petition under this same section) — so a description of this section as reaching only grandparents would understate who it actually authorizes to petition.

GRANDPARENT VISITATION WITHIN A PENDING CUSTODY PROCEEDING — FAMILY CODE § 3103
Separately from a freestanding petition, California Family Code § 3103(a) provides: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a grandparent of a minor child of a party to the proceeding if the court determines that visitation by the grandparent is in the best interest of the child." This pathway is available only inside an already-pending proceeding of the kind described in § 3021 (for example, a dissolution, legal separation, or other custody-related proceeding between Riley Lee's parents) — not as its own standalone filing. Under § 3103(c), the person petitioning must give notice of the petition to each of Riley Lee's parents, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of Riley Lee, by certified mail, return receipt requested, to that person's last known address, or to the parties' attorneys of record. Under § 3103(d), a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof applies that grandparent visitation is not in Riley Lee's best interest if Riley Lee's parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a grandparent of a minor child of a party to the proceeding if the court determines that visitation by the grandparent is in the best interest of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3103(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3103.)
  "The petitioner shall give notice of the petition to each of the parents of the child, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of the child, by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, to the person's last known address, or to the attorneys of record of the parties to the proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3103(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3103.)
  "There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the child's parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(d) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3103(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3103.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's separate, pending-custody-proceeding grandparent visitation mechanism (distinct from the freestanding petition addressed in this document's other clauses) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3103(a), (c), and (d)); no additional independent source beyond § 3103 itself was found for this. The cross-referenced definition of a "proceeding described in Section 3021" is not independently restated in full here.

THE GENERAL GRANDPARENT VISITATION PETITION AND ITS TWO REQUIRED FINDINGS — FAMILY CODE § 3104(A)
California's most frequently used grandparent-visitation mechanism, Family Code § 3104(a), lets a grandparent petition the court directly, without any other custody proceeding pending between Riley Lee's parents. The court may grant reasonable visitation to Casey Lee only if it makes both of two required findings: first, that there is a preexisting relationship between Casey Lee and Riley Lee that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in Riley Lee's best interest; and second, a balancing of Riley Lee's interest in having visitation with Casey Lee against the right of Riley Lee's parents to exercise their parental authority. Family Code § 3104(c) requires Casey Lee, as petitioner, to give notice of the petition to each of Riley Lee's parents, any stepparent, and any person with physical custody of Riley Lee, by personal service under Code of Civil Procedure § 415.10.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court does both of the following: (1) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the grandparent and the grandchild that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child. (2) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the grandparent against the right of the parents to exercise their parental authority."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  "The petitioner shall give notice of the petition to each of the parents of the child, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of the child, by personal service pursuant to Section 415.10 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two-finding standard and notice requirement governing California's general, freestanding grandparent visitation petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that meeting these two findings alone is sufficient to obtain visitation. A separate statutory filing restriction and separate rebuttable presumptions — addressed in this document's companion clauses — can bar this petition from being filed at all, or can reverse the burden of proof, even where these two findings would otherwise be met. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3104(a) and (c)); no additional independent source beyond § 3104 itself was found for this.

THE STATUTORY BAR ON FILING A § 3104 PETITION WHILE PARENTS ARE MARRIED AND LIVING TOGETHER
Family Code § 3104(b) states that "A petition for visitation under this section shall not be filed while the natural or adoptive parents are married," unless one or more of six specific circumstances exist: the parents are currently living separately and apart on a permanent or indefinite basis; one parent has been absent for more than a month without the other spouse knowing that parent's whereabouts; one parent joins in the petition with the grandparent; the child is not residing with either parent; the child has been adopted by a stepparent; or one parent is incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized. If a change of circumstances occurs such that none of these six circumstances any longer exist, § 3104(b) directs that a parent may move the court to terminate grandparental visitation, and the court "shall grant the termination." The U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57 held that a state visitation statute affording no deference at all to a fit parent's own decision about a child's visitation can violate that parent's substantive due process right under the Fourteenth Amendment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A petition for visitation under this section shall not be filed while the natural or adoptive parents are married, unless one or more of the following circumstances exist: (1) The parents are currently living separately and apart on a permanent or indefinite basis. (2) One of the parents has been absent for more than one month without the other spouse knowing the whereabouts of the absent spouse. (3) One of the parents joins in the petition with the grandparents. (4) The child is not residing with either parent. (5) The child has been adopted by a stepparent. (6) One of the parents is incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized. At any time that a change of circumstances occurs such that none of these circumstances exist, the parent or parents may move the court to terminate grandparental visitation and the court shall grant the termination."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  "In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children."
  — Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (U.S. Supreme Court, plurality opinion of O'Connor, J.), 530 U.S. 57, 66 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1087668/troxel-v-granville/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, together with a real U.S. Supreme Court decision, used as real evidence of a specific statutory filing restriction and of the constitutional backdrop against which it operates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that Troxel itself construed or struck down this particular California provision (it did not; Troxel addressed a Washington statute, Wash. Rev. Code § 26.10.160(3), not this one). This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: California's actual text does not describe the married-and-living-together scenario as a "rebuttable presumption" against visitation — it is a flat bar on filing the § 3104 petition at all while the parents are married, subject to the six listed exceptions above. The distinct rebuttable presumptions that do exist under § 3104 apply to different fact patterns (the parents agreeing that visitation should not be granted, or a sole-custody parent objecting to it) and are addressed in this document's companion clause, together with the case law actually construing those presumptions. This clause's two citations — a single statutory subsection, § 3104(b), and the Troxel opinion — are independent of one another.

THE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTIONS AGAINST GRANDPARENT VISITATION UNDER SECTION 3104(E)-(F), AND CALIFORNIA'S APPLICATION OF TROXEL
Beyond the filing restriction described in this document's companion clause, Family Code § 3104 creates two further, distinct rebuttable presumptions against grandparent visitation. Under § 3104(e), there is a rebuttable presumption that grandparent visitation is not in Riley Lee's best interest if Riley Lee's natural or adoptive parents agree that Casey Lee should not be granted visitation rights. Under § 3104(f), a separate rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof applies if the parent who has been awarded sole legal and physical custody of Riley Lee in another proceeding — or the parent with whom Riley Lee resides if there is currently no operative custody order — objects to visitation by Casey Lee. In Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57, the U.S. Supreme Court's plurality opinion cited California's § 3104(e) presumption approvingly, contrasting it with the Washington statute struck down in that case, as an example of a state law that gives a fit parent's own decision a "presumption of validity." The California Supreme Court later confirmed, in In re Marriage of Harris (2004) 34 Cal.4th 210, that where a sole-custody parent objects to grandparent visitation, § 3104(f)'s presumption controls, is constitutional both on its face and as applied, and requires the trial court to actually apply it rather than simply asking what visitation schedule serves the child's best interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "There is a rebuttable presumption that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the natural or adoptive parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(e) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  "There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the parent who has been awarded sole legal and physical custody of the child in another proceeding, or the parent with whom the child resides if there is currently no operative custody order objects to visitation by the grandparent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(f) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3104(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3104.)
  "Cf., e.g., Cal. Fam. Code Ann. § 3104(e) (West 1994) (rebuttable presumption that grandparent visitation is not in child's best interest if parents agree that visitation rights should not be granted)"
  — Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (U.S. Supreme Court, plurality opinion of O'Connor, J.), 530 U.S. 57, 70 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1087668/troxel-v-granville/)
  "Because the mother had sole custody of the child and objected to grandparent visitation, Family Code section 3104, subdivision (f), imposed a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that grandparent visitation was not in the child's best interest. The superior court did not utilize this presumption."
  — In re Marriage of Harris, 34 Cal.4th 210 (2004) (California Supreme Court, majority opinion of Moreno, J.), 34 Cal.4th 210, 216 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2623596/in-re-marriage-of-harris/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and two real appellate decisions, used as real evidence of the specific rebuttable presumptions Family Code § 3104 creates and of how California courts have applied Troxel's constitutional floor to them — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3104(e) and (f)); the Troxel and Harris citations are independent of that statutory source and of each other. This clause corrects a further assumption in the research request that prompted it: no single statutory or case-law "presumption against grandparent visitation when the parents are married and living together and object" was located as such. Troxel's own opinion cites § 3104(e) — the parents-agree presumption — and Harris's holding addresses § 3104(f) — the sole-custody-parent-objects presumption; both are materially different fact patterns from two married, cohabiting parents who both object to a petition, which instead falls under the flat filing bar in § 3104(b) addressed in this document's companion clause, not under either presumption described here.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — GRANDPARENT VISITATION PETITION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual grandparent-visitation petition filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not grant visitation rights; only a court order does that.]

At any time that a change of circumstances occurs such that none of these circumstances exist, the parent or parents may move the court to terminate grandparental visitation and the court shall grant the termination.

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the filing restriction described in this document's companion clause, Family Code § 3104 creates two further, distinct rebuttable presumptions against grandparent visitation. Under § 3104(e), there is a rebuttable presumption that grandparent visitation is not in Riley Lee's best interest if Riley Lee's natural or adoptive parents agree that Casey Lee should not be granted visitation rights. Under § 3104(f), a separate rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof applies if the parent who has been awarded sole legal and physical custody of Riley Lee in another proceeding — or the parent with whom Riley Lee resides if there is currently no operative custody order — objects to visitation by Casey Lee. In Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57, the U.S. Supreme Court's plurality opinion cited California's § 3104(e) presumption approvingly, contrasting it with the Washington statute struck down in that case, as an example of a state law that gives a fit parent's own decision a "presumption of validity." The California Supreme Court later confirmed, in In re Marriage of Harris (2004) 34 Cal.4th 210, that where a sole-custody parent objects to grandparent visitation, § 3104(f)'s presumption controls, is constitutional both on its face and as applied, and requires the trial court to actually apply it rather than simply asking what visitation schedule serves the child's best interest.
